section_summary.extract_value: This section reports gender-split path analyses on a single dataset (women n = 199; men n = 200). The hypothesised model fit poorly for both genders and modified models provided good fit for women and adequate fit for men; bootstrapped indirect effects (5,000 samples) indicated multiple significant indirect pathways to body appreciation via self-esteem and connectedness to nature, with some gender-specific differences. The section displays and references modified models for women (Fig. 2) and men (Fig. 3) and reports fit indices and confidence intervals for indirect effects.
section_summary.evidence_source: Note: Women n = 199, Men n = 200. The hypothesised model did not fit these data well in women, χ2 = 413.136, p < .001; df = 26; χ2_{normed} = 15.890; CFI = .379; SRMR = .227; RMSEA = .274 with 90% CI = .251 – .298, or in men, χ2 = 547.392, p < .001; df = 26; χ2_{normed} = 21.054; CFI = .334; SRMR = .224; RMSEA = .317 with 90% CI = .295 – .341. The modified model for women is displayed in Fig. 2 and provided good fit to the data, χ2 = 16.129, p = .013; df = 6; χ2_{normed} = 2.688; CFI = .958; SRMR = .065; RMSEA = .092 with 90% CI = .039 – .148. Bootstrapping procedures were used to obtain bias-corrected confidence intervals for the indirect effect, drawing on 5000 bootstrap samples from the dataset.

section_summary.extract_value: This section reports path analysis results comparing women and men (women n = 199; men n = 200), noting the hypothesised model initially did not fit but modified models provided good/adequate fit for women and men respectively. Bootstrapped indirect effects (5000 samples) are reported for multiple paths, and Table 2 presents bivariate correlations with women represented above the diagonal and men below the diagonal.
